questions.prompt: What does `: ~Copyable` mean on a Swift `struct` or `enum`?

options.text: The type turns off Copyable and cannot be copied implicitly.
options.explanation: Right. A ~Copyable type enforces unique ownership so values move instead of copying.

options.text: The type is allocated on the heap and managed by ARC.
options.explanation: Wrong. ~Copyable structs and enums stay value types with no reference counting.

options.text: The type cannot define any stored properties or methods.
options.explanation: Wrong. ~Copyable structs can have stored properties, methods, and deinit.

options.text: The type disables Swift 6 strict concurrency checks.
options.explanation: Wrong. ~Copyable controls copying and ownership, not concurrency isolation.

questions.prompt: Which two Swift types can be declared as noncopyable with `: ~Copyable`?

options.text: Classes and actors
options.explanation: Wrong. Reference types use ARC and are shared, not noncopyable value types.

options.text: Structs and enums
options.explanation: Right. Only structs and enums can be declared as noncopyable with ~Copyable.

options.text: Protocols and classes
options.explanation: Wrong. Classes cannot use ~Copyable; protocols only let ~Copyable types conform.

options.text: Actors and tuples
options.explanation: Wrong. Actors are reference types and tuples cannot use : ~Copyable.

questions.prompt: Why can a `~Copyable` struct define a `deinit` while a regular struct cannot?

options.text: Because ~Copyable structs always inherit from NSObject.
options.explanation: Wrong. Structs never inherit from classes.

options.text: Because regular structs are immutable and never leave scope.
options.explanation: Wrong. Regular structs leave scope too, but they can be copied freely.

options.text: Because a ~Copyable value has one unique owner, so deinit runs once.
options.explanation: Right. Single ownership guarantees cleanup runs once when the unique value ends.

options.text: Because Swift automatically turns ~Copyable structs into classes.
options.explanation: Wrong. Noncopyable structs remain value types.

questions.prompt: What does the `borrowing` keyword do on a function parameter?

options.text: It moves ownership permanently into the function.
options.explanation: Wrong. Moving ownership permanently is what consuming does.

options.text: It allows the function to mutate the caller's variable directly.
options.explanation: Wrong. Exclusive write access uses inout or mutating.

options.text: It creates an automatic copy before entering the function.
options.explanation: Wrong. borrowing avoids copying and disables implicit copies inside the body.

options.text: It grants temporary read-only access and lets the caller keep the value.
options.explanation: Right. The callee reads the value temporarily without taking ownership.

questions.prompt: What happens to a caller's `~Copyable` variable after passing it to a `consuming` parameter or method?

options.text: Ownership moves away and using the variable again is a compile error.
options.explanation: Right. Consuming transfers ownership, so the caller cannot access the variable afterward.

options.text: The caller can still read it, but cannot mutate it.
options.explanation: Wrong. The caller loses all access once the value is consumed.

options.text: Swift makes a deep copy so both caller and callee own separate copies.
options.explanation: Wrong. A ~Copyable type cannot be copied; ownership transfers instead.

options.text: The variable becomes nil at runtime.
options.explanation: Wrong. Unless it was Optional and set to nil, non-optional values cannot be used again.

questions.prompt: What does `discard self` do inside a `consuming` method on a `~Copyable` type?

options.text: It returns self back to the caller.
options.explanation: Wrong. A consuming method takes ownership and cannot return self via discard.

options.text: It destroys self immediately without running deinit.
options.explanation: Right. discard self ends self and suppresses deinit after manual cleanup.

options.text: It calls deinit twice to flush buffers.
options.explanation: Wrong. discard self prevents deinit from running at all.

options.text: It marks the method as mutating instead of consuming.
options.explanation: Wrong. discard self is only valid inside consuming methods.

questions.prompt: Which ownership modifier gives temporary exclusive write access without permanently consuming the value?

options.text: borrowing
options.explanation: Wrong. borrowing only permits read-only access.

options.text: consuming
options.explanation: Wrong. consuming transfers ownership permanently and ends caller use.

options.text: inout or mutating
options.explanation: Right. inout and mutating lend exclusive write access and return ownership afterward.

options.text: discard self
options.explanation: Wrong. discard self destroys self inside a consuming method.

questions.prompt: How do you allow a generic function `func log<T>(_ value: borrowing T)` to accept a `~Copyable` type?

options.text: Change the parameter type to Any.
options.explanation: Wrong. Any requires Copyable by default and boxes values.

options.text: Mark the function with @Sendable.
options.explanation: Wrong. Sendable relates to concurrency, not copyability.

options.text: Use <T: Copyable> on the generic parameter.
options.explanation: Wrong. T already defaults to Copyable; that keeps excluding ~Copyable types.

options.text: Write <T: ~Copyable> on the generic parameter.
options.explanation: Right. Suppressing Copyable lets the generic parameter accept both copyable and noncopyable types.

questions.prompt: What happens when you write `let b = a` where `a` is a `~Copyable` struct?

options.text: Ownership moves from a to b, and a cannot be used afterward.
options.explanation: Right. Assignment moves a noncopyable value instead of duplicating it.

options.text: Swift makes a shallow copy of a into b.
options.explanation: Wrong. ~Copyable suppresses copying on assignment.

options.text: Both a and b share a heap reference.
options.explanation: Wrong. A ~Copyable struct stays a value type with a single owner.

options.text: The assignment fails unless you mark b as weak.
options.explanation: Wrong. weak applies to class references, not ~Copyable structs.

questions.prompt: Why does Swift disable implicit copies inside a `borrowing` parameter even for `Copyable` types?

options.text: Because Copyable types cannot be copied inside functions.
options.explanation: Wrong. You can still copy explicitly with the copy keyword.

options.text: To guarantee no hidden copies occur unless you explicitly write copy.
options.explanation: Right. Writing borrowing or consuming stops accidental retains or copies in performance code.

options.text: Because borrowing turns a String into a pointer.
options.explanation: Wrong. String stays a safe Swift value with borrowing semantics.

options.text: To force every parameter to use inout.
options.explanation: Wrong. borrowing is read-only and separate from inout.

questions.prompt: Can a `~Copyable` type be wrapped in Swift's `Optional` type (like `VaultState?`)?

options.text: No, Optional only works with Copyable types.
options.explanation: Wrong. Swift 6 updated Optional (SE-0427 and SE-0437) so Wrapped can be ~Copyable.

options.text: Only if VaultState is a class.
options.explanation: Wrong. VaultState is a noncopyable struct or enum.

options.text: Yes, Optional supports ~Copyable wrapped values.
options.explanation: Right. You can wrap ~Copyable values in Optional and unwrap them with consume.

options.text: Only in Swift 5 mode, not Swift 6 mode.
options.explanation: Wrong. Swift 6 fully supports Optional with ~Copyable values.

questions.prompt: What does `protocol Resource: ~Copyable` allow that `protocol Resource` does not?

options.text: It lets classes skip implementing required methods.
options.explanation: Wrong. Conforming types still implement all protocol requirements.

options.text: It makes every conforming type a singleton.
options.explanation: Wrong. Multiple instances can exist, each with one owner.

options.text: It automatically adds deinit to every conforming type.
options.explanation: Wrong. Types define their own deinit when needed.

options.text: It lets both Copyable and ~Copyable types conform to Resource.
options.explanation: Right. Suppressing Copyable on a protocol allows noncopyable types to conform.

questions.prompt: What happens when you switch over a `borrowing` `~Copyable` enum in modern Swift?

options.text: You can borrow associated values in patterns without consuming the enum.
options.explanation: Right. Borrowing pattern matching lets you inspect enum cases and keep using the value.

options.text: The switch always destroys the enum immediately.
options.explanation: Wrong. Borrowing switches inspect associated values without consuming the enum.

options.text: Enums cannot conform to ~Copyable at all.
options.explanation: Wrong. Both structs and enums can be ~Copyable.

options.text: Each case automatically copies the associated payload.
options.explanation: Wrong. Noncopyable payloads cannot be copied; they are borrowed or consumed.

questions.prompt: Why would you use `consume` on a normal `Copyable` value like a large `Array`?

options.text: To convert the Array into a class reference.
options.explanation: Wrong. consume does not change a type from struct to class.

options.text: To move ownership without copying and end use of the old binding.
options.explanation: Right. consume ends the old binding and avoids an extra retain or copy.

options.text: To allow mutating a let constant in place.
options.explanation: Wrong. consume moves the value out rather than mutating a let binding.

options.text: To run deinit on the Array elements immediately.
options.explanation: Wrong. consume transfers ownership; elements stay alive in the new owner.

questions.prompt: What is a common real-world reason to choose a `~Copyable` struct over a `class` for a file handle?

options.text: Classes cannot run code inside deinit.
options.explanation: Wrong. Classes have had deinit since Swift 1.

options.text: Classes cannot hold integer file descriptors.
options.explanation: Wrong. Classes can store any property type.

options.text: It prevents accidental sharing and catches double-close bugs.
options.explanation: Right. You avoid ARC overhead and prevent double-close bugs at compile time.

options.text: A ~Copyable struct skips all Swift 6 type checking.
options.explanation: Wrong. The compiler strictly checks ~Copyable ownership rules.

questions.prompt: In 2–5 sentences, explain the difference between `borrowing` and `consuming` parameters on a `~Copyable` type in Swift.

rubric.criterion: States that borrowing grants temporary read-only access without copying or taking ownership
States that consuming moves ownership into the function and ends caller access
Notes that the caller can still use the value after a borrowing call

questions.modelAnswer: A borrowing parameter gives a function temporary read-only access without copying or taking ownership, so the caller can keep using the value afterward. A consuming parameter moves ownership into the function. Once consumed, the caller cannot access that variable again.

questions.prompt: In 2–5 sentences, explain why `~Copyable` structs can define `deinit` and when you should call `discard self`.

rubric.criterion: Explains that single ownership ensures deinit runs once on a ~Copyable struct
Explains that discard self inside a consuming method destroys self without running deinit
Gives a clear reason such as avoiding double cleanup after an explicit close

questions.modelAnswer: A ~Copyable struct has only one owner, so Swift knows it can run deinit exactly once when the value leaves scope. Inside a consuming method like close(), you call discard self to destroy the value immediately and skip deinit. This prevents cleanup code from running twice.

questions.prompt: In 2–5 sentences, explain how generics and protocols work with `~Copyable` types, and give a syntax example.

rubric.criterion: States that generic parameters and protocols require Copyable by default
Explains writing <T: ~Copyable> or protocol Name: ~Copyable to opt in
Shows a valid syntax example such as func inspect<T: ~Copyable>(_ x: borrowing T)

questions.modelAnswer: By default, every Swift generic parameter and protocol requires Copyable. To accept noncopyable types, you suppress that default requirement with ~Copyable, such as protocol Resource: ~Copyable. For example, writing func inspect<T: ~Copyable>(_ item: borrowing T) lets the function accept both copyable and noncopyable values.

questions.prompt: In 2–5 sentences, explain why `borrowing` and `consuming` can be useful on regular `Copyable` types and how the `copy` keyword helps.

rubric.criterion: States that borrowing and consuming avoid extra copies or ARC retains in hot paths
Explains that implicit copies are disabled inside those parameters
States that the copy keyword makes an explicit copy when needed

questions.modelAnswer: On normal Copyable types like String or Array, borrowing and consuming parameters stop Swift from making hidden copies or extra ARC retains. Because implicit copies are turned off inside those parameters, the compiler catches accidental copying. If you actually need a duplicate, you write copy value explicitly.

questions.prompt: In 2–5 sentences, compare using a `~Copyable` struct versus a `class` when modeling a unique resource like a database transaction.

rubric.criterion: States that a ~Copyable struct stays a value type without heap allocation or ARC overhead
Explains that ~Copyable enforces single ownership and catches use-after-consume at compile time
Notes that a class allows shared references and relies on runtime checks to guard double commits

questions.modelAnswer: A ~Copyable struct stays a value type with no heap allocation or ARC reference counting. The compiler enforces single ownership, so calling commit() as a consuming method prevents reusing or double-committing the transaction at compile time. A class allows shared references, so preventing double commits requires runtime state flags.
